food.text: The Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ is the oldest known cookbook from the Iberian Peninsula, and its full title refers to cooking in the Maghreb and Al-Andalus in the era of the Almohads. It is believed to have been composed in the 12th or 13th centuries and contains 462 recipes.
Meat dominates the Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ, with 311 recipes dedicated to various types of meat. The book also includes a significant number of sweet dishes, many of which incorporate honey.

Makroudh is a Maghrebi cookie filled with dates and nuts or almond paste, and its name derives from its diamond shape. According to historian Daniel Newman, the oldest known recipe is in a 13th-century Arabic cookbook by Ibn Razīn al-Tujībī and describes date-filled, fried dough.
The Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ showcases both elite and common dishes. Vegetarian dishes make up 14% of its savory recipes, which makes the book stand out.

The Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ begins with quotations from the classical writers Hippocrates and Galen on the importance of appetite and taste. It blends cooking with medical knowledge, and its author is believed to be an educated Andalusian who knew both fields well.

The invasion of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym Arabs in the 11th century spread Bedouin nomadism in areas where agriculture was previously dominant. As Arab nomads spread, the territories of the local Berber tribes were moved and shrank: the Zenata were pushed to the west, the Kabyles to the north, and the Berbers took refuge in the mountains while the plains were Arabized. The Berber population had to share pastures and seasonal migration paths with the newcomers.

The Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ includes six explicitly Jewish recipes, plus a recipe for braided bread similar to modern challah. Other recipes, such as sfenj, reflect culinary practices shared by both Jews and Muslims.
Medieval Tunisian oases had a holiday dish called barkukishto. It was prepared with dried octopus and small fish in a vegetable broth.

In Tunisian Arabic, tabil means seasoning, though earlier it only meant ground coriander. Paula Wolfert makes the plausible claim that it is one of the spice mixes brought to Tunisia by Muslims coming from Andalusia in 1492 after the fall of Granada.

After the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492, North Africa, predominantly Morocco, became the primary refuge, but the refugees faced hardship. Solomon ibn Verga recorded instances of starvation during which people resorted to eating grass.

According to Hélène Jawhara Piñer, the earliest known version of mofletta appears in the Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ as a sweet dish called murakkaba. Pancakes are cooked on one side only, stacked into a small tower, and drizzled with melted butter and honey. This method is unique within the cookbook.

art.text: The riad is a garden courtyard divided into four quadrants by two paved paths that cross at the center, where a fountain usually stands. The earliest known true riad in Morocco was in the Almoravid palace built by Ali ibn Yusuf in Marrakesh in the early 12th century.

Moorish architecture became a shared style across the Maghreb and al-Andalus because the Almoravids and the Almohads unified both regions for much of the 11th to 13th centuries. Major centers of artistic development included Fes, Marrakesh, Tunis and Tlemcen.

Zellij, a mosaic of cut tiles, became commonplace in Moorish architecture from the 13th century onward. It often shows geometric patterns of intersecting straight lines rotated to form radiating, star-like designs.

When the Almoravids conquered al-Andalus in the 11th century, they commissioned Muslim, Christian and Jewish artisans from there to work on monuments in Morocco and across their empire. This created a shared architectural and artistic heritage between al-Andalus and North Africa.

The Almoravids and the dynasties after them, including the Almohads and Marinids, perfected the riad garden and made it a standard feature of palace architecture. It was especially common in Marrakesh, where climate and available space suited bourgeois mansions and royal palaces.

The Madrasa Tashfiniya in Tlemcen was founded by Abu Tashfin I, who reigned from 1318 to 1337. It was celebrated for its rich decoration, including zellij tiles with sophisticated arabesque and geometric motifs that were later repeated in some Marinid monuments.

The Zayyanid founder Yaghmorasan, who ruled from 1236 to 1283, added minarets to the Mosque of Agadir and the Great Mosque of Tlemcen. His successor Abu Sa'id 'Uthman founded the Mosque of Sidi Bel Hasan in 1296.
The Great Mosque of Constantine was originally constructed by the Hammadids in the 12th century. They built it on the ruins of a Roman temple.

During his siege of Tlemcen at the start of the 14th century, the Marinid leader Abu Ya'qub built a fortified settlement nearby called al-Mansurah. It includes the monumental Mansurah Mosque, begun in 1303 and only partly preserved today.

A description of the Hafsid Ras al-Tabya palace near the present-day Bardo in Tunis, from the second half of the 15th century, records a large cruciform garden with a central fountain. It also had four water features and four pavilions arranged in a cross, much like riad palaces elsewhere.

war.text: In the 11th century the Fatimids, rulers of Egypt, sent Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal westward into North Africa as retribution against the Zirids, who had proclaimed their independence, become increasingly independent and abandoned Shia Islam. To persuade the Bedouin to go, the Fatimid caliph gave each tribesman a camel and money, and a severe drought in Egypt also pushed them west. Historians estimate that 50,000 to 250,000 Arab nomads migrated to the Maghreb, though some scholars propose substantially higher numbers.

In 1270, during the Eighth Crusade, Christian forces captured the fortress at Carthage, which Muslim forces had garrisoned until the Hafsid period. After the Crusaders withdrew, the Hafsid ruler Muhammad I al-Mustansir decided to destroy it completely to prevent a repetition.

The Banu Hilal quickly defeated the Zirids after the battle of Haydaran, and the Zirids abandoned Kairouan to take refuge on the coast, where they survived for a century. The Banu Hilal also deeply weakened the neighboring Hammadid dynasty and the Zenata. Ibn Khaldun noted that the lands ravaged by Banu Hilal invaders had become completely arid desert.
Finding the Banu Hilal's continued presence intolerable, the Almohad Caliphate defeated them in the Battle of Setif. Many of them were forced to leave Ifriqiya and settle in Morocco.

The Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym spread onto the high plains of Constantine, where they gradually obstructed Qal'at Bani Hammad just as they had done to Kairouan a few decades earlier. From there they gradually gained control over the high plains of Algiers and Oran. Ibn Khaldun noted that the lands ravaged by Banu Hilal invaders had become completely arid desert, and their influx spread nomadism into areas where agriculture had previously been dominant.

To weaken resistance by Arab tribes in Ifriqiya, the Almohad ruler Abd al-Mu'min transferred them to Morocco in large numbers in the 12th century. He settled them in the Atlantic plains, and the Arab tribes increasingly played an important role in the politics of the Almohad Empire.

As Arab nomads spread across the Maghreb in the 11th century, the territories of the local Berber tribes were moved and shrank. The Zenata were pushed to the west and the Kabyles to the north, and the Berbers took refuge in the mountains while the plains were Arabized. The article says the Fatimids had set these Arabs upon the Berbers as punishment for their former Zirid Berber clients, who defected and abandoned Shiism.

The Almoravids fought a war against the Barghawata, whom they considered heretics, and the Barghawata's Atlantic lands were largely destroyed and depopulated. The Almohads then depopulated the region again with expeditions in 1149–1150 and 1197–1198, sent to suppress revolts against them there.

According to Ibn Khaldun, the Banu Hilal came to the Maghreb with their wives and children, and settled in Ifriqiya after winning battles against Berber tribes. Abu Zayd al-Hilali is said to have led between 150,000 and 300,000 Arabs into the region, who intermarried with the indigenous peoples.

In the second half of the 12th century the Banu Hilal pushed on into the Moulouya valley and the Atlantic coast of the western Maghreb, reaching areas such as Doukkala. Their advance across North Africa had begun in Libya, Tunisia and Algeria.

literature.text: One Hundred and One Nights is a book of Arabic literature made up of twenty stories, and it resembles the far more famous One Thousand and One Nights. Its origin is a mystery. Some suggest Persia or India, but the stories are said to come from the Maghreb.

Rawd al-Qirtas is a popular and influential medieval history of the Maghreb. It is commonly presumed to have been written by Ibn Abi Zar, who died between 1310 and 1320. It was said to have been written at the instigation of the Marinid Sultan Abu Sa'id Uthman II.

After the massacre of 1391 in Spain, the rabbi Simon ben Zemach Duran fled to Algiers and became its chief rabbi. He wrote influential works on Jewish law, philosophy and science. One of them, Magen Avot, covers physiology, psychology and natural philosophy.
In 2010 the Orientalist Claudia Ott discovered the oldest known manuscript of One Hundred and One Nights. It is dated to 1234 or '35 and includes 85 nights.

Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 found refuge mostly in Morocco, and some wrote about the hardships that followed. Solomon ibn Verga recorded starvation so severe that people ate grass. Judah ibn Hayyat described burrowing into garbage heaps to escape the cold.

Only a few stories are shared between One Hundred and One Nights and One Thousand and One Nights: the frame story of Scheherazade, The Ebony Horse and the Seven Viziers. Everything else differs, though the themes and structure are very similar. Scholars see the two collections as complementing each other.

The name of the author of Rawd al-Qirtas is uncertain, and so is his authorship of the work. Many variant manuscripts have circulated since the Middle Ages. Very little is known about him beyond the fact that he was evidently a scholar at Fes.

science.text: Ibn al-Yasmin, a Maghrebi mathematician born in Fez, made a crucial contribution to developing Ghubari numerals, the West Arabic numerals now used in most parts of the world. He was educated in both Fez and Seville and died in 1204.

Ibn al-Banna' al-Marrakushi, born in Marrakesh in 1256, was a Moroccan polymath who wrote over 100 works on subjects including astronomy, mathematics, logic, and meteorology. He worked as a mathematician, astronomer, and astrologer until his death in 1321.

In 1147 the Almohad ruler Abd al-Mu'min conquered Marrakesh from the Almoravids. He is reported to have demolished all the mosques in the city built under the Almoravids, purportedly because their qibla alignment was wrong. He then ordered the Almoravid minbar moved into his new Kutubiyya Mosque, which suggests he saw it as a trophy. A hidden mechanism let the wooden pulpit advance and retract from its storage room seemingly on its own, and contemporary observers marvelled at it.

Little is known about Ibn al-Yasmin's personal life beyond that he was born into a Berber family. Despite this, his work developing Ghubari numerals made him an influential mathematician of the medieval Maghreb before his death in 1204.

Ibn al-Banna' studied under at least 17 masters in Marrakesh and Fez, learning subjects ranging from the Quran and Arabic grammar to arithmetic and Euclid's Elements. This broad education reflected the depth of scientific learning available in the medieval Maghreb.

The minbar later installed in Marrakesh was actually built far away in Cordoba, where production began in 1137 under the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf and took about seven years to finish. It was then shipped in pieces and reassembled in the Almoravid capital.

The physician Ibn Zuhr began his medical career serving as court physician for the Almoravid empire. After falling out of favor with the ruler Ali bin Yusuf bin Tashufin, he fled Seville and was apprehended and jailed in Marrakesh in 1140.

Ibn al-Banna' al-Marrakushi's Talkhīṣ ʿamal al-ḥisāb, or Summary of Arithmetical Operations, covered topics such as fractions and the sums of squares and cubes. It was one of more than 100 works he wrote on subjects ranging from mathematics to astrology.

Ibn al-Banna' owed his name, meaning the son of the mason, to his father's trade, even though he became one of Marrakesh's leading scholars. He taught students in the city, including Abd al-Aziz ibn Ali al-Hawari al-Misrati, who died in 1344.
tags: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ali al-Hawari al-Misrati

politics.text: The Almoravids emerged from a coalition of nomadic Berber tribes in what is now Mauritania and the Western Sahara. They founded Marrakesh as a capital around 1070, and their empire stretched over the western Maghreb and al-Andalus. It ended in 1147, when the Almohads captured Marrakesh and killed the last Almoravid ruler, Ishaq ibn Ali.

In 1121 or so, Ibn Tumart was recognized by his followers as the Mahdi and set up his base at Tinmel in the Atlas Mountains. After his death, Abd al-Mu'min founded the Almohad caliphate. In 1147 he conquered Marrakesh after an eleven-month siege and declared himself caliph; the last Almoravid ruler was killed. By 1159 the Almohads ruled all of the Maghreb.

The Marinids, a Berber Zenata dynasty, overthrew the Almohads by capturing Marrakesh in 1269. At the height of their power in the mid-14th century, under Abu al-Hasan and his son Abu Inan, they briefly held sway over most of the Maghreb, including large parts of modern Algeria and Tunisia.

Hammad ibn Buluggin declared himself emir at the start of the 11th century, splitting the Zirid domains into two dynasties. Under Emir Al Nasir, the Hammadid emirate briefly became the most important state in the Maghreb, stretching from Tlemcen in the west to Tunis in the east.

After the 11th century the Maghreb was most often divided into three states, roughly matching Morocco, western Algeria, and eastern Algeria with Tunisia. It was only occasionally and briefly unified, as under the Almohad Caliphate, the Fatimids and the Zirids. The Hammadids also managed to conquer land in all the countries of the region.

The Almoravid victory at the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086 helped halt Christian kingdoms in Iberia. It united the Maghreb and al-Andalus politically for the first time. Their rulers never claimed the title of caliph.

Between 1067 and 1072, the Hammadid emir al-Nasir built Béjaïa, turning a small fishing village into a large, fortified town and port. Al-Nasir had come to power after his paternal cousin Buluggin ibn Muhammad, who had invaded northern Morocco and briefly taken Fez for a few months in 1062, was assassinated by al-Nasir himself, who then succeeded him as emir. By the early 12th century Béjaïa had about 100,000 people.

The Zirids ruled Ifriqiya from 972 to 1148, at first as emirs in the name of the Fatimids. In 999 the sons of Ziri ibn Manad, shut out of power, rebelled against Badis ibn al-Mansur; they were defeated in battle and most of the brothers were killed. The only remaining brother of stature, Zawi ibn Ziri, led the surviving rebels west to al-Andalus, where he founded the Taifa of Granada in 1013. The Almoravids conquered that kingdom in 1090.

The Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen became independent around 1236 as Almohad rule collapsed, under Yaghmurasen Ibn Zyan. Facing the Marinid threat, he allied with the Sultan of Granada and King Alfonso X of Castile. The Marinids besieged Tlemcen for eight years, until 1307.

In September 1090, Yusuf ibn Tashfin forced Granada to surrender and exiled Abdallah ibn Buluggin to Aghmat. Maliki jurists in al-Andalus supported the Almoravids, criticizing the Taifa kings as impious and illegitimate. In September 1091, al-Mu'tamid surrendered Seville, after allying with Alfonso VI had further undermined his popular support.

In 1016 or 1017, the new Zirid emir al-Mu'izz ibn Badis launched a pogrom against the remaining Isma'ilis in Ifriqiya. The Zirids had begun distancing themselves from Cairo, and relations grew more strained under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim over disputes about Cyrenaica and Tripoli.

The Wattasids were de facto rulers between 1420 and 1459 while officially acting as regents or viziers. When Sultan Abdalhaqq II tried to break their power, he carried out a massacre of the Wattasid family in 1459, though two Wattasids survived. In 1465 he appointed a Jewish vizir, Aaron ben Batash, which provoked a popular revolt in Fez. The revolt overthrew him and he was murdered, his throat cut, ending Marinid rule.

After the Crusaders who had captured Carthage's fortress during the Eighth Crusade in 1270 withdrew, Muhammad I al-Mustansir decided to destroy it completely. The aim was to prevent any repetition of the capture by a hostile power.

philosophy.text: Islamic philosophy is said to have begun with al-Kindi and declined with Ibn Rushd, also known as Averroes, in the late 12th century. His death effectively ended the Islamic peripatetic school. Philosophical activity then declined significantly in the west of the Islamic world, including al-Andalus and the Maghreb.

The Almohad movement began with Ibn Tumart, who was recognized by his followers as the Mahdi around 1121, a declaration that was effectively a declaration of war on the Almoravid state. He set up his base at Tinmel in the Atlas Mountains, which served as the movement's spiritual center and military headquarters. His movement fought a guerilla war in the mountains for eight years, then grew into an empire that controlled much of the Maghreb.

Even as philosophy declined in the west of the Islamic world, Ibn Khaldun made important contributions to the philosophy of history in his Muqaddimah. His work stands out in a region where the older philosophical schools had faded.

Ibn Tumart, a Masmuda Berber born in 1077, went on pilgrimage to Mecca and then studied. He came back to the Maghrib inspired by the teachings of al-Ash'ari and al-Ghazali, and he preached an interior awareness of the Unity of God.

The Almohads were called al-Muwahhidun, meaning the Unitarians. Their founder Ibn Tumart was a puritan and hard-edged reformer who gathered a strict following among the Berbers of the Atlas. He founded a radical community and eventually began an armed challenge to the Almoravids.

The Almohad caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur was a highly accomplished man who wrote a good Arabic style. He protected the philosopher Averroes. Yet the Almohad rulers under whom he governed had at first driven many Jewish and Christian subjects to flee to Portugal, Castile and Aragon, and the Almohads rejected the dhimmi status and publicly burned Maliki books.

Averroes (1126–1198) rejected the thought of al-Ghazali and turned to a detailed study of Aristotle. He commented on most of Aristotle's works, and his commentaries did much to guide the interpretation of Aristotle in later Jewish and Christian scholastic thought.

After fleeing to Algiers, Simon ben Zemach Duran became chief rabbi. He wrote influential works on Jewish law, philosophy and science, including Magen Avot, which covers physiology, psychology and natural philosophy.

After the massacre of 1391 in Spain, Jewish refugees and conversos moved from Iberia and Mallorca to Morocco and Algeria. They included notable rabbis such as Isaac ben Sheshet and Simon ben Zemach Duran, who brought Jewish learning to the Maghreb.

In 1055, at the request of Sijilmasa's elders after 60 years of Maghrawa rule, Abdallah ibn Yasin, spiritual leader of the Almoravid movement, brought his new army to Sijilmasa and killed the Maghrawa leader, Mas'ud ibn Wanudin al-Maghrawi, according to al-Bakri. The Almoravids then imposed an extremely strict interpretation of Islam, smashing musical instruments and closing down wine shops throughout the city.

Under the Almohads, local Christians came under pressure, and the record shows persecutions and demands that the Christians of Tunis convert to Islam. In 1159 the Almohad Abd al-Mu'min forced the Christians and Jews of Tunis to convert.

culture.text: In the 11th century a huge wave of Bedouin tribes from the Arabian Peninsula, including the Banu Hilal, Banu Sulaym and Maqil, came into the Maghreb after numerous battles with the Berbers, such as the Battle of Haydaran. They destroyed the Berber Zirid state and most of its cities, sparing only the coastal strip at al-Mahdiyya. According to Ibn Khaldun, the lands the Banu Hilal ravaged became completely arid desert. Historians call it the most significant event in the medieval history of the Maghreb.

From the end of the 7th century, the peoples of the Maghreb converted to Islam over more than 400 years. Christianity declined from the 10th century, and by the end of the 11th century only two bishops were left, in Carthage and Hippo Regius. Pope Gregory VII (1073-85) consecrated a new bishop for Hippo.

Maghrebi Jews thrived in major urban centers under early Muslim rule, but they also faced periods of persecution, notably under the Almohad Caliphate. After the 1391 massacre in Spain, Jewish refugees and conversos moved from Iberia to Morocco and Algeria.
Under the Marinid dynasty (1244-1465), Arabic became both the common and official language in Morocco. Many Berber groups were Arabized, and the Zenata were heavily assimilated into Arab culture.

The Almohad movement was founded by Ibn Tumart, a Masmuda Berber from the Atlas mountains who became the mahdi. A puritan and hard-edged reformer, he preached an interior awareness of the Unity of God. He gathered a strict following among the Berbers in the Atlas.

The Almohad caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur wrote a good Arabic style and protected the philosopher Averroes. According to the research of Muhammad al-Manuni, there were 400 paper mills in Fez during his reign in the 12th century.

Christianity in the Maghreb seems to have suffered several shocks that led to its demise. Many upper-class, urban-dwelling, Latin-speaking Christians left for Europe after the Muslim conquest, and the large-scale conversions to Islam from the end of the 9th century followed. Many Christians of a much reduced community departed the Maghreb in the mid-11th century, and remnants were evacuated in the 12th by the Norman rulers of Sicily. The Latin-African language lingered a while longer.

Berber Christians continued to live in Tunis and Nefzaoua in southern Tunisia until the early 15th century. Ibn Khaldun hinted at a native Christian community in the villages of Nefzaoua, who paid the jizya and had some people of Frankish descent among them. In the first quarter of the fifteenth century, the native Christians of Tunis even extended their church.

Morocco became the main refuge for Jews expelled from Spain in 1492. Solomon ibn Verga recorded starvation in which people ate grass, while Judah ibn Hayyat described burrowing into garbage heaps to escape the cold.
